summary: Brick 1898 light on North Head at the Columbia River mouth, Washington; first-order lens moved from Cape Disappointment; keepers to 1961; state park since 2012.

lens.note: First-order Fresnel from 1898 (transferred from Cape Disappointment); fourth-order Fresnel from 1937; revolving searchlight 1950 (2014 brochure)

structures.note: Conical masonry tower. 65 ft (19.8 m) per NRHP, keepers' history and 2014 brochure; USLHS record gives 50 ft from base to lantern center and dressed stone with brick lining. Sources do not reconcile.

access.note: Washington State Parks describes the lighthouse as open to the public.

stay.note: Keepers' residence near the light is available for overnight stays (Washington State Parks)

facts.agency: Washington State Parks and Recreation Commission (since 2012); US Coast Guard maintains the light

events.note: First-order light authorized by act of 15 February 1893 (no appropriation that year)
$25,000 toward a first-order light, sundry civil act of 18 August 1894
Erection contract made 8 September 1896; keepers' history says construction began 1897
Lit 16 May 1898; first-order Fresnel lens moved from Cape Disappointment
First-order Fresnel lens transferred from Cape Disappointment
Lens framework braced; call-bell system installed between dwellings and tower (fiscal 1899)
Columbia River light-vessel No. 50 broke away 29 Nov 1899 and went ashore near McKenzie Head, between North Head and Cape Disappointment
Weather station reopened at North Head in August 1902
Schooner Frank W. Howe wrecked at Seaview, 22 February 1904; North Head weather observer raised the alarm
Wild duck broke a storm pane (April); slight damage to the lens
Fourth-order Fresnel lens replaced the first-order lens; rotated by electricity (2014 brochure)
Fresnel lens replaced by a revolving searchlight (2014 brochure)
Automated in 1961 per historical marker and roster ('at least 1961')
Transferred to Washington State Parks on 22 October 2012 (NPS brochure); Coast Guard keeps the light

corrections.why: USLHS record gives 192.5 ft above mean high water (58.67 m); OSM value 194 is not a metre figure for this light
NRHP, keepers' history and the 2014 brochure give 65 ft (19.8 m). The USLHS record gives 50 ft from base to lantern center; a human should resolve the conflict before any change.
Historical marker and roster give automation in 1961; roster lists keepers to at least 1961

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The fiscal 1897 Board report shows contracts let in September 1896 with delays into 1897; the keepers' history gives construction starting in 1897, completion in April 1898 and lighting on 16 May 1898. Both dates fit a 1896 contract and 1897 erection, but neither source says so directly.
Record values 59.0, 58.67 and 59.1 m are close; USLHS gives 192.5 ft (58.67 m). The OSM value (194) is not consistent with the others.
NRHP, keepers' history and the 2014 brochure give 65 ft; the USLHS record gives 50 ft from base to lantern center. The story states both.

notes_for_editor: Roster names from the USLHS place page (NARA registers via Kraig Anderson), matched by name and position (0.20 km). Names are as printed; the keepers' history uses 'Alex K. Pesonen'. The roster page was checked against every keeper in the story: principal, first and second assistant lines all match. The Board's fiscal 1898 report is not in the local corpus; its penalty figures are quoted second-hand from the keepers' history (footnoted as such). Tower height conflict: NRHP, keepers' history and the 2014 brochure give 65 ft; the USLHS record gives 50 ft from base to lantern center and dressed stone with brick lining. The story states both. Lens prehistory: the NRHP says the first-order lens was first built in France in 1822 and used in a New England lighthouse; the 2014 brochure says it was stationed in 1841 at Navesink, New Jersey, before San Francisco and Cape Disappointment. Not in the story; for a human to check. The NPS-hosted 2014 brochure is a Washington State Parks publication; footnoted so. The NPS brochure says Mabel E. Bretherton 'served as a lighthouse keeper for many years'; the roster and the keepers' history give 1905-1907 at North Head; the brochure may mean her whole career. Transfer date: 2014 brochure gives 22 October 2012; Wikipedia (not cited) says November 2012. Coast Guard's own history page could not be read (archived copy returned 403/wrapper only); the automation year rests on the historical marker and roster. Newspaper search for North Head keepers ('Pesonen', 'North Head light') returned unrelated pages; none used. The 1904 Frank W. Howe report gives the weather observer as Mr. Kelliher; not matched to other records. The Frank W. Howe account: the report says the seven aboard were taken off, and the captain said two of his crew had been lost earlier (overboard and from the rigging), so the story gives both. The 1900 light-vessel entry is at scan p. 226 (page index confirmed). The NRHP nomination is a district nomination; North Head data are on pages 2-4 of its description. Current climbing or tour rules for the tower are not stated in the sources read; the story says so.
